headline: Demand weakened again in the third quarter as rates neared 7%, and builders began walking away from optioned lots.
national: Four builders have filed since the last edition: Lennar and KB Home for quarters ended August 31, PulteGroup and M/I Homes for September 30. All four describe the quarter as weaker than the one before it. Every one delivered fewer homes than a year earlier (Lennar down 3%, Pulte down 9%, KB down 19%, M/I down 2%) and took fewer net orders (Lennar down 9%, Pulte down 6%, KB down 12%, M/I down 2%). Margins are still compressed year over year: Lennar 15.8% against 17.5%, Pulte 24.8% against 26.2%, KB 16.5% against 18.2%, M/I homebuilding 18.4% against 21.5%. Lennar and KB did improve on their second quarters.

Rates are the stated cause. Lennar puts the 30-year mortgage at about 7% and the 10-year Treasury near 5%, up from 6.4% to 6.5% earlier in the year, and ties the move to energy-driven inflation from tension with Iran. M/I says mortgage rates topped 7% by quarter end, and Pulte says they rose sharply, most of all in September. Resale competition is building at the same time. KB says resale inventory is at its highest level in a decade with prices trending down in several of its markets, and Lennar reports rising resales in Texas and Florida.

Cancellations moved up in the middle of the group. Pulte held at 16%, Lennar rose to 15% from 14%, KB to 18% from 17%, and M/I sat at 12.3% against 12.2%. Alongside Horton's 20% and Toll's 2.6% from the last edition (June and July quarters), the gradient still sorts by buyer segment, but the entry-level and first move-up builders are converging on Horton rather than on Toll.

Incentives are now pulling in two directions. Lennar's fell again, to 12.0% of revenue from 14.3% a year earlier and 12.9% in its prior quarter, although its West segment went the other way. M/I's incentives and closing costs rose to $73.2 million from $53.5 million, with mortgage rate buydowns up $23.2 million, and Pulte expects its incentives to stay elevated. Nobody is building into it. Pulte's unsold homes in production fell to 6,627 from 7,369 and its completed specs to 1,696 from 2,027. KB delivered 74% built-to-order and posted its first year-over-year backlog increase in four years. Lennar guides fourth-quarter orders of 19,500 to 20,500 against deliveries of 22,000 to 23,000, converting inventory to cash.
land: The new development this quarter is builders using the option to exit. KB abandoned 8,777 previously controlled lots in its first nine months; its lots owned or controlled fell 5% to 61,581 since November, and the share held under option fell to 40% from 43%. Pulte says it has walked away from a number of land option agreements and is re-underwriting options before buying more land. Its controlled lots fell to 224,275 from 234,632 at year end, with 55% optioned against 57%, and its third-quarter land-related charges rose to $37.5 million from $27.6 million.

Lennar stays at the land-light extreme: 11,808 homesites owned against 476,153 controlled, 98% of the total, and the total is down from more than 511,000 a year ago. About 86% of its third-quarter deliveries came through land banking. The cost of that model is now visible. Lennar says land cost per home has risen, partly through option maintenance fees on extended deal durations, and expects that to weigh on margin while it works through positions underwritten under earlier market conditions. M/I controls about 48,900 lots, roughly five years of supply and 3% fewer than a year ago, with 25,509 of them under option at an aggregate $1.74 billion.

They are still buying selectively. KB put $722.3 million into land in the quarter, up 40% from a year earlier, and ended with 277 communities, up 5%. Pulte's average community count rose 7%, and M/I expects to finish the year about 5% higher. Toll, from the last edition, held 75,500 lots with 58% under option.

The land pricing note has turned more cautious. The last edition carried Pulte's second-quarter comment that land inflation was easing. Its third-quarter 10-Q says instead that it continues to face pressure in the cost of land acquisition and development, and KB, M/I and Lennar all name higher land or lot costs as a margin drag. None of these four filings reports falling land prices.
socal: The filings do speak to California this quarter, through each builder's western segment, and the read splits by builder.

Lennar's West segment, which includes California, is its weakest. Gross margin was 12.1% against 16.3% a year earlier, the lowest of its four segments, and the filing cites lower average prices in California among other states from base price cuts and more incentives. West deliveries fell 8% to 4,529 and orders 9% to 4,319. It is also the one Lennar segment where incentives rose, to 10.9% of revenue from 10.5%.

Pulte's West segment, which also includes California, had closings down 18%, orders down 15% and a 21% cancellation rate, the highest of its six segments, and pre-tax income fell 57%. Average price rose 2% only because of closing mix in its California markets. West is where Pulte owns most of its land: 25,681 lots owned against 12,447 optioned, the reverse of its company-wide split.

KB's West Coast segment (California, Idaho and Washington) is the exception. Net orders rose 8% to 937, backlog value rose 22% to $1.02 billion, average community count rose 25% to 111, and the cancellation rate improved to 16% from 18%. Prices are giving: average selling price fell 6% to $641,800 and segment gross margin slipped to 16.7%. KB carries 20,471 West Coast lots at $3.21 billion, its largest land position by value. M/I has no California operations.

One structural change: Sumitomo Forestry completed its acquisition of Tri Pointe on May 14, 2026 at $47 per share, delisting the company and making the group roughly the fifth largest U.S. builder at about 15,000 units annually. Tri Pointe reports Homebuilding Southern California as a named segment, so one of the most active regional counterparties is now a private subsidiary of a Japanese parent. Expect a different capital posture and no more quarterly segment disclosure.
ventura: No public builder discloses at county level. Ventura appears in none of these filings. Anything county-specific attributed to a builder filing is extrapolation.

The resale side, from Redfin's September county data in the resale panel on this board: median sale price $873,795, up 3.7% from a year earlier, on 513 sales, up 3.5%, with a 51-day median time on market and sales at 98.5% of list. The forward-looking pieces are softer. Pending sales were down 9.1% year over year, active listings up 4.2%, and months of supply at 3.7. That is the early local version of what the builders describe nationally.
From the last edition: KB Home is actively selling at Beltramo Ranch in the county, and the new-home pipeline countywide is thin for a county of this size.

The two items that belong on the radar are regulatory, not corporate. The 2025 California Building Standards Code and local County amendments took effect for all applications submitted on or after January 1, 2026, and AB 1308 now requires the County to inspect completed residential work of one to ten units within ten business days, with a miss treated as a Housing Accountability Act violation. That second one is real leverage on close-out timing.
takeaway: Four more filings, all weaker, strengthen the case against entitling entry-level detached product for a near-term sale. Finished lots in attainable price ranges are still the gap, but builders will now pay for them only on option terms they can walk away from.

Expect re-trades and walk-aways on options underwritten in 2024 and 2025. KB's 8,777 abandoned lots and Pulte's walk-aways are the evidence, and Lennar's rising option fees show the land bankers are pricing the extensions. For a land seller, deposit and extension terms now matter as much as headline price.

In California, KB's West Coast segment is the one builder book adding communities and orders. Horton's 20% cancellation rate from the June quarter is still the weakest signal in the group; its fiscal-year 10-K, due in November, is the next read that matters for anyone holding a PSA with it.
